title: The Great Silence
paragraphs: In 1950, during a lunchtime conversation at Los Alamos, the physicist Enrico Fermi is said to have asked a deceptively simple question: where is everybody? His reasoning, as later reconstructed, ran roughly as follows. The Milky Way contains a vast number of stars, many of them far older than the Sun, and even a civilisation that travelled slowly could, in principle, spread across the galaxy in a period that is short compared with its age. If intelligent life were at all common, some sign of it ought to be obvious by now.

The paradox is not a proof that we are alone, and it is worth being precise about what it assumes. In 1961 the astronomer Frank Drake wrote down an equation that breaks the question into factors, from the rate at which stars form to the fraction of planets on which life arises and the length of time a technological society remains detectable. Astronomers now have reasonable estimates for the first few terms; observations from missions such as Kepler suggest that planets are common. The later terms, however, remain almost entirely guesswork.

Proposed resolutions divide into broad families. Some suggest that life, or at least complex life, is genuinely rare, perhaps because some improbable step lies between simple chemistry and intelligence. Others propose that civilisations tend not to last, or that they choose not to expand or communicate. A more modest group argues that the silence is less surprising than it seems, because our searches have covered only a small portion of the sky and the radio spectrum, for a few decades.

What makes the question unusually uncomfortable is that some of these answers concern our own future. If the improbable step lies behind us, our existence is remarkable; if it lies ahead, the silence may be a warning.
